key_insight: Patient data in EMRs predicted 30-day bloodstream-infection mortality well, but adding large-scale microbial genes and proteins did not meaningfully improve prediction.
clinical_relevance: For risk stratification in bloodstream infection, host and clinical features appear far more useful than microbial trait profiling for estimating short-term mortality.
method: Analyzed 35,746 bloodstream infections from Calgary, Canada (2006–2022).
Combined microbial genomes, quantitative proteomes, and electronic medical record data.
Compared machine-learning mortality models with and without >70,000 microbial genes/proteins.
evidence_signal: EMR-based models achieved an AUC of 0.83 for 30-day mortality, and performance did not improve when microbial features were added.
watch_item: Microbial factors may cluster with specific patient cohorts, so associations can be confounded and should not be treated as independent predictors.
paper_title: Microbial traits have minimal power for predicting death from bloodstream infection
